axiom

AK-see-um -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, AK. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Axiom is a statement that is self-evidently true.

The coach ran the whole team on one simple axiom: whoever works hardest in practice starts on Friday.

Example

Before the club's first debate, the members write one line on the whiteboard that nobody in the room would argue with -- 'a rule that cannot be enforced is not really a rule' -- and every argument that follows is built on top of it.

That opening line is an axiom: a statement so self-evidently true that the group accepts it without proof and reasons forward from there. An axiom is not a conclusion you argue toward; it is the ground you stand on while arguing.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

truism: A truism is a statement so obviously true that saying it adds nothing -- 'winners score more points than losers.' An axiom is obvious too, but it earns its keep: a whole argument or system is built on top of it. A truism just sits there; an axiom holds something up.

principle: A principle is a general rule you choose to reason or act from, like 'hear both sides before deciding.' An axiom is narrower and firmer: a statement everyone in the discussion already accepts as plainly true, used as the fixed starting point of an argument. A principle guides; an axiom anchors.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

falsehood: a statement that is not true

conjecture: a guess that has not been proven

Where it sits · how formally it anchors an argument — maxim → axiom → postulate

maxim vs. axiom: A maxim is smaller and homier than an axiom -- 'measure twice, cut once' is handy advice, while an axiom is a foundation stone that a whole argument or system rests on.

postulate vs. axiom: Postulate is axiom's technical twin and carries the most formal weight: an axiom is accepted because it is plainly true, while a postulate is laid down on purpose at the start of a proof so everything after it can be tested.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — axi-

root — axi-: worthy (Greek axios)

suffix — -oma

suffix — -oma: the thing that results (Greek -oma)

Put it together

Put it together: Axiom comes from Greek axioma, 'that which is thought worthy,' built on axios, 'worthy.' An axiom is literally a statement worthy of acceptance -- so clearly true that a thinker grants it without demanding proof.

Use the root in a new word: axiomatic

Use the root in a new word: axiomatic: It is axiomatic in any kitchen that a dull knife is more dangerous than a sharp one.

Word Building

Word Choice

Axiom belongs to mathematics, logic, and formal argument: the axioms of geometry, a founding axiom, an axiomatic assumption. Reach for it when you mean a starting truth that nobody in the discussion disputes. If the statement still needs proving, it is a claim or a hypothesis -- not an axiom.
